problem: Graph-based planning over learned distance metrics (SoRB, SPTM) stores every or randomly subsampled state, so the graph has O(|V|^2) edges and many infeasible ones. The planner exploits these faulty edges, so plans are brittle and do not scale to large environments.
motivation: Long-horizon goal-conditioned control from raw images needs a graph memory that stays compact and accurate. Visually similar states can be far apart in action space (perceptual aliasing), so a purely perceptual similarity is not a valid criterion for merging nodes. The paper needs a principled, goal-conditioned aggregation criterion that keeps the graph sparse and its errors correctable.
key_idea: Build a sparse graph memory by merging states only when they are interchangeable both as goals and as starting states under the learned asymmetric distance (two-way consistency), then prune faulty edges with k-NN filtering and self-supervised cleanup.
insight: Sparsity is what makes error correction feasible: with a dense graph the number of faulty edges is too large to remove by test-time cleanup, whereas with the sparse TWC graph success rises quickly during cleanup (Fig. 6). In the SafetyGym ablation (Table 3), two-way consistency beats uniform subsampling, perceptual-only, and one-way (incoming or outgoing) criteria both before and after cleanup (38.2% and 92.9% vs 31.2% and 64.6% for uniform). Theorem 1 shows the increase in plan length is bounded by 2kτ, which grows only linearly with the merging threshold.
method: Two-way consistency (TWC): states s1 and s2 are redundant if C_out = max_ω|d(s1,ω)-d(s2,ω)| ≤ τ_a and C_in = max_s'|d(s',s1)-d(s',s2)| ≤ τ_a. This extends approximate Q-irrelevance to goal-conditioned settings with an asymmetric distance.

Greedy online graph construction (Alg. 1): make one pass over the replay buffer and add a state only if it fails TWC against every node already in the graph. Add edges with d ≤ MAXDIST and weight them with d. A perceptual-consistency L2 embedding check (β-VAE or a distance subnetwork) is used as a fast path to skip TWC checks.
k-NN edge filtering: limit each node to its k nearest successors, so the worst-case number of faulty edges grows linearly rather than quadratically in the node count.
Self-supervised cleanup: at test time, sample random goals and plan with Dijkstra. If the low-level agent cannot reach the next waypoint, delete that edge and replan.

Semi-parametric hierarchy: the graph planner picks waypoints, and a low-level controller (D3PG actor / SPTM behavior-cloned visual controller) executes them. Distances come from a distributional Q-function ensemble, a Siamese ResNet-18 classifier, or a contrastive bilinear metric. Distances are aggregated pessimistically over temporal windows to reduce aliasing.
Theory: Theorem 1 shows the shortest path in the TWC graph is at most 2kτ_a longer than in the dense graph, and at most kε+2kτ_a from the true distance if d has error ε.

setting.backbone: SoRB (D3PG actor/critic ensemble, trained from scratch) in PointEnv; SPTM Siamese ResNet-18 distance plus behavior-cloned visual controller (pretrained, distance finetuned) in ViZDoom; conv-net contrastive distance, β-VAE and proprioceptive controller (trained from scratch) in SafetyGym
setting.training_data: Self-collected exploration: 100 random-action episodes of 200 steps (20,100 images) in ViZDoom, plus replay buffers in PointEnv and SafetyGym. No external data.
setting.observation: PointEnv: (x,y) coordinates. ViZDoom: first-person RGB images. SafetyGym: 64x64 first-person RGB (odometry available for observations but not for goals).
setting.action_space: PointEnv and SafetyGym: continuous control; ViZDoom: discrete. The high level selects graph waypoints.
setting.privileged: none at test time (goal given as an image or coordinate; ground-truth distance is used only to define difficulty bins for evaluation)

numbers_note: The text says SGM solves SafetyGym with a 96.6% success rate, while Table 1 and Table 3 give 92.9%. The table values are recorded above. The benchmarks are custom environments and not canonical navigation benchmarks. Baselines from Table 1: SoRB 28.0, SPTM 39.3, ConSPTM 68.2.
results: SGM improves every graph-based baseline: SoRB 28.0% → 100%, SPTM 39.3% → 60.7% (ViZDoom), ConSPTM 68.2% → 92.9% (SafetyGym), about 2.1x on average. Cleanup improves mean performance by 2.4x. Plans take fewer steps, and action selection is about 7x faster than SoRB (0.077 s vs 0.550 s).
limitations: Performance is still limited by perceptual aliasing in ViZDoom (60.7%) and degrades with goal difficulty (26% on hard goals).
Graph construction needs quadratically many TWC evaluations, and the greedy set-cover approximation is heuristic. Thresholds are environment-specific and tuned by hand.
Evaluated only in simulated mazes and only with the reward of reaching the goal, ignoring safety during intermediate steps. Not tested on real robots or manipulation.
